drills.q: Which HTTP header carries a gRPC client's deadline to the server?
drills.a: grpc-timeout, part of the HTTP/2 metadata for the call.

drills.q: Name the four gRPC RPC shapes.
drills.a: Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.

drills.q: Which HNSW parameter is the only one that can be tuned live, per query, without rebuilding the index?
A team deploys a gRPC service behind a Kubernetes Service with 5 replicas but observes one pod handling 90% of traffic. Diagnose.
drills.a: gRPC multiplexes many RPCs over a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection; if the Service uses plain L4 (connection-level) load balancing, it routes once at connection establishment and pins ALL subsequent RPCs on that connection to the same pod. Fix: client-side round_robin load balancing resolving multiple addresses, or an L7-aware proxy like Envoy balancing individual streams.

drills.q: A worker pool is implemented as `for _, item := range items { go process(item) }` with no cap. Under a traffic spike, what breaks, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Goroutine count and any downstream connections/resources those goroutines hold grow without limit, exhausting this service's memory and potentially the downstream's capacity simultaneously -- there's no backpressure. Fix: a fixed-size pool of workers reading from a bounded channel, which blocks the producer (real backpressure) once the pool is saturated.

drills.q: Explain why raising efSearch after a vector index re-index sometimes fails to restore recall to its prior level.
drills.a: efSearch only widens the query-time candidate search -- it cannot compensate for a structurally lower-quality graph if efConstruction was reduced at build time, since the graph's actual connections (chosen once, during build, based on efConstruction's candidate breadth) are already fixed. Check and fix efConstruction, not just efSearch.

drills.q: Design the choice: efSearch value for a live, p99-latency-sensitive user search endpoint vs a background batch re-ranking job with no hard latency constraint.
drills.a: Live endpoint: lower efSearch tuned to hit the latency SLA, accepting somewhat lower recall as the tradeoff. Batch job: much higher efSearch to maximize recall, since total throughput/wall-clock time matters more than any single query's latency -- or better, expose efSearch as a client-controllable request parameter so callers set their own tradeoff instead of the service hardcoding two fixed profiles.

drills.q: A client reports frequent DeadlineExceeded errors against a gRPC server whose own p99 latency looks fine in isolation. Walk through the diagnosis in order.
drills.a: First check whether the client's own configured deadline is realistic given the server's actual p99 (a 200ms client timeout against a 300ms server p99 fails correctly, nothing wrong server-side). Second, check whether the deadline budget is being correctly reduced at each hop in a multi-service chain rather than reused unshrunk. Third, only after ruling those out, investigate genuine server-side tail latency causes: a slow dependency, GC pauses, or connection-pinning load-balancing (uneven pod traffic) concentrating load on one instance.

drills.q: When would you justify building a custom Go microservice wrapping a native HNSW library instead of using a managed vector database, and what do you give up by doing so?
drills.a: Justified when profiling proves the managed DB's network hop and query-abstraction overhead is the actual bottleneck against a genuinely tight latency budget, or per-traffic-class efSearch control is needed that the managed API doesn't expose. You give up persistence/durability, replication, native filtered-search support, and operational tooling (backups, monitoring, scaling) the managed option provides out of the box -- all of which the custom service must now build and operate itself.

drills.q: Why does errgroup's fail-fast, first-error-wins cancellation model sometimes NOT fit a coordination need, and what would you reach for instead?
drills.a: errgroup cancels all sibling goroutines the moment any one returns an error, which is wrong when you need to collect ALL errors from a batch (e.g. reporting every failed item in a bulk operation) or want remaining independent work to continue despite one failure. In that case, hand-roll coordination with a WaitGroup and a channel/slice collecting every error instead of relying on errgroup's shared-cancellation-on-first-error behavior.
